Content:
The average rate of change of the function [MATH: y=f(x)] on the interval [MATH: [a,a+h]] is given by
[MATH: \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}.]

Content:
This can be interpreted as the slope of the secant line that intersects the curve at the points [MATH: \color{blue}P] and [MATH: {\color{red}Q},] as shown below.

Graphic:

Content:
The instantaneous rate of change of the function [MATH: f(x)] at the point [MATH: x = a] is the limit of the average rate of change as [MATH: h \to 0.] It is denoted by [MATH: f'(a)] and given by

Content:
[MATH: f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac {f(a+h) - f(a)} {h}.]

Content:
Geometrically, as [MATH: h \to 0], the point [MATH: \color{red}Q] moves along the curve [MATH: y=f(x)] towards the point [MATH: {\color{blue}P},] and the secant transforms into the line that touches the curve at exactly one point [MATH: ({\color{blue}P}).] That line is called the tangent line to the curve [MATH: y=f(x)] at the point [MATH: \color{blue}P.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c19ad835d91bf88422f3058e68885970]

Content:
The value of [MATH: f'(a)] is equal to the slope of the tangent line to the curve [MATH: y=f(x)] at [MATH: x=a.]

sections.readable_text: Find the instantaneous rate of change of [MATH: f(x)=3x^2] at the point [MATH: x=5] using the definition.

sections.normalized_html:
Let's use the definition

[MATH: f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac {f(a+h) - f(a)} {h}.]

In our problem, we have [MATH: a=5], and so by the definition we have

[MATH: f^{′}(5) = lim_(h → 0)(f(5 + h) − f(5))/(h).]

Applying this to [MATH: f(x)=3x^2], we get

[MATH: f^{′}(5)|= lim_(h → 0)((3(5 + h)^{2} − 3(5)^{2})/(h)); = lim_(h → 0)((75 + 30h + 3h^{2} − 75)/(h)); = lim_(h → 0)((30h + 3h^{2})/(h)); = lim_(h → 0)(30 + 3h); = 30 + 3(0); = 30.]

sections.normalized_html: Using the limit of a difference quotient, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve [MATH: y=2x-x^2] at the point [MATH: x=2.]
sections.readable_text: Using the limit of a difference quotient, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve [MATH: y=2x-x^2] at the point [MATH: x=2.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(x)=2x-x^2.] The slope of the tangent line is equal to [MATH: f'(2).]

Let's use the equivalent definition for [MATH: f'(a),] given by

[MATH: f'(a) = \lim_{x\to a}\dfrac {f(x) - f(a)} {x-a}.]

Using the above definition with [MATH: a=2,] we have [MATH: f'(2) = \lim_{x\to 2}\dfrac {f(x) - f(2)} {x-2}.]

Applying this to [MATH: f(x)=2x-x^2,] we get [MATH: f^{′}(2)|= lim_(x → 2)(([2x − x^{2}] − [2(2) − (2)^{2}])/(x − 2)); = lim_(x → 2)((− x^{2} + 2x)/(x − 2)); = lim_(x → 2)((− x(x − 2))/(x − 2)); = lim_(x → 2)(− x); = − 2.]

So the slope of the tangent line to the curve at [MATH: x=2] is [MATH: -2.]

Item 6 — Example: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point Using the Equivalent Definition

Example Prompt:
Using the limit of a difference quotient, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve [MATH: y=2x-x^2] at the point [MATH: x=2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(x)=2x-x^2.] The slope of the tangent line is equal to [MATH: f'(2).]

Let's use the equivalent definition for [MATH: f'(a),] given by

[MATH: f'(a) = \lim_{x\to a}\dfrac {f(x) - f(a)} {x-a}.]

Using the above definition with [MATH: a=2,] we have
[MATH: f'(2) = \lim_{x\to 2}\dfrac {f(x) - f(2)} {x-2}.]

Applying this to [MATH: f(x)=2x-x^2,] we get
[MATH: f^{′}(2)|= lim_(x → 2)(([2x − x^{2}] − [2(2) − (2)^{2}])/(x − 2)); = lim_(x → 2)((− x^{2} + 2x)/(x − 2)); = lim_(x → 2)((− x(x − 2))/(x − 2)); = lim_(x → 2)(− x); = − 2.]

So the slope of the tangent line to the curve at [MATH: x=2] is [MATH: -2.]
